summary: Defines Exclusive XML Canonicalization, a way of serializing an XML subdocument that leaves out ancestor context. This matters when a digital signature on an XML piece must stay valid after it is moved out of its original message or into another one. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two copies of the same text can be written in slightly different ways. This gives one exact way to write a piece of XML so a signature still matches after you copy it elsewhere.

questions: xml signatures when moving a subdocument
how to keep signatures valid when moving xml
subtitle: A way to serialize XML fragments that remain valid when moved to a different context

tldr.problem: When an XML fragment is signed and then removed from its original message and inserted into a different one, the standard canonical XML method includes ancestor namespace context, which changes and breaks the signature.
tldr.mechanism: Exclusive XML Canonicalization serializes XML subsets while excluding ancestor context that is not actively used by the fragment itself, keeping namespace declarations minimal and ensuring portability.
tldr.outcome: A signed XML fragment can be moved between documents without invalidating its signature, which is essential for protocol messages that assemble fragments from multiple sources.

today: RFC 3741 is an Internet Standard and the definitive specification for exclusive XML canonicalization, widely used in XML digital signature and encryption standards.

sections.title: The Problem of Moving Signed XML
sections.content:
The Canonical XML Recommendation specifies a standard way to serialize XML so that semantically equivalent documents are bit-for-bit identical. However, canonical XML includes ancestor context, meaning it pulls in namespace declarations and attributes from parent elements. This causes a problem in applications that move XML fragments, such as when a protocol extracts a signed message part and uses it in a different message.

Exclusive XML Canonicalization solves this by excluding ancestor context that is not visibly used by the fragment itself. Two key rules differ from standard canonicalization: XML namespace attributes (like xml:lang and xml:space) are not imported into orphan nodes, and namespace nodes outside an explicit InclusiveNamespaces PrefixList are rendered only where they are visibly used and not already in effect from an output ancestor.
sections.plainLanguage: Regular XML canonicalization is like photocopying with all the margins and page numbers. Exclusive canonicalization is like photocopying just what matters.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
The specification uses several precise terms. A document subset is a portion of an XML document indicated by an XPath node-set. An apex node is an element in the subset that has no element ancestors in the subset. An orphan node is an element whose parent is not in the subset. The output parent of an orphan is the nearest ancestor element in the subset; apex nodes have no output parent.

An element visibly utilizes a namespace declaration if the element or one of its attribute nodes uses that namespace prefix. The InclusiveNamespaces PrefixList is a parameter listing namespace prefixes to handle using standard canonical XML rules, allowing the caller to explicitly include context when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The method tracks which pieces of an XML document are in the fragment, which ones are missing, and which namespaces are actually being used.

sections.title: The Exclusive Canonicalization Method
sections.content:
Exclusive XML Canonicalization is identical to Canonical XML except for four key differences. First, it does not search ancestor nodes for xml: namespace attributes to copy into orphan elements. Second, it accepts an optional InclusiveNamespaces PrefixList parameter. Third, a namespace node is rendered only if its parent element is in the node-set, it is visibly utilized, and either it has not been rendered by an ancestor or the nearest ancestor rendering it has a different value.

Fourth, when rendering the default namespace (xmlns=""), the method outputs it only if the element visibly uses the default namespace, has no default namespace node in the subset, and an output ancestor that uses the default namespace does have one in the node-set.
sections.plainLanguage: The method carefully tracks which namespace declarations a fragment actually needs, ignoring declarations from ancestor elements unless the fragment is explicitly told to keep them.

sections.title: Use in XML Digital Signatures
sections.content: Exclusive canonicalization is identified by the URIs http://www.w3.org/2001/10/xml-exc-c14n# and http://www.w3.org/2001/10/xml-exc-c14n#WithComments (for including XML comments). It is used as a Transform or CanonicalizationMethod algorithm in XML Digital Signature and XML Encryption. A Transform element can include an InclusiveNamespaces element with a PrefixList attribute listing prefixes to treat inclusively, using the format dsig soap #default for prefixes and the #default token for the default namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: When you digitally sign an XML piece, you choose this method as your canonicalization. You can say which namespace prefixes should follow the old inclusive rules if you need them to.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Requirements
sections.content:
This specification has two main limitations. First, XML being canonicalized may depend on xml:lang, xml:space or xml:base attributes from ancestors. These MUST either be explicitly provided in the fragment where needed, or declared with equivalent values in every context where the fragment will be used.

Second, attributes whose values are XPath expressions or QNames may depend on namespace prefixes that are not visibly used. The solution is either to make the prefix visible in the fragment, declare the namespace identically in all contexts, or add the prefix to the InclusiveNamespaces PrefixList. Additionally, applications must carefully specify how removed and reinserted fragments handle default namespace declarations to avoid confused interpretation in a new context.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is not foolproof. You have to be careful about special XML attributes and about how namespaces are named in attribute values that are not tags.
